title: One Health Insights From Pteropus medius: Nipah Virus Spillover, Microbiota, and Antimicrobial Resistance.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review examines the relationship among Nipah virus (NiV) spillover, Pteropus medius bat microbiota, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) within a One Health framework, focusing on Bangladesh where NiV causes recurrent fatal encephalitis outbreaks.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar to identify relevant peer-reviewed studies published between 2006 and 2025.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Pteropus medius populations harbor clinically important resistant bacteria, including ESBL-producing Escherichia coli, Salmonella spp., and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus spp. Habitat fragmentation, wastewater contamination, urbanization, agricultural intensification, and increased human-wildlife interactions are major drivers facilitating both NiV spillover and AMR dissemination.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies bidirectional exchange of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) among wildlife, livestock, and humans in bat roosts near agricultural lands, wastewater discharge sites, and peri-urban settlements, though specific mechanisms and quantitative data on ARG transfer remain limited.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Integrated One Health surveillance and environmental management strategies are recommended to mitigate future zoonotic and AMR threats in Bangladesh, emphasizing the need for comprehensive monitoring of bat-associated microbiota and environmental contamination.

analysis.summary_en: This narrative literature review examines the relationship among Nipah virus (NiV) spillover, Pteropus medius bat microbiota, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) within a One Health framework in Bangladesh. The review identifies that Pteropus medius populations harbor clinically important resistant bacteria, including ESBL-producing E. coli, Salmonella spp., and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus spp. Major drivers facilitating both NiV spillover and AMR dissemination include habitat fragmentation, wastewater contamination, urbanization, agricultural intensification, and increased human-wildlife interactions. The review also notes bidirectional exchange of antimicrobial resistance genes among wildlife, livestock, and humans in bat roosts near agricultural and peri-urban areas. The findings highlight the importance of integrated One Health surveillance and environmental management strategies to mitigate future zoonotic and AMR threats in Bangladesh.

title: W730A PERTURBS MOLECULAR RECOGNITION IN THE NIPAH VIRUS POLYMERASE INHIBITOR POCKET: DYNAMICS OF BMS-986205 AND ERDRP-0519

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed how the W730 residue in the Nipah virus polymerase inhibitor pocket influences molecular recognition of two antiviral chemotypes, BMS-986205 and ERDRP-0519. It aimed to clarify the structural and energetic consequences of removing W730’s indole chemistry on ligand binding.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research used computational modeling to compare wild-type and W730A mutant Nipah virus polymerase inhibitor pockets in complex with BMS-986205 and ERDRP-0519. A 100-compound screen provided selection context, and paired docking defined starting poses for explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations.
analysis.methods: Explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations were performed for each ligand with wild-type and W730A polymerase. Analyses included ligand displacement, protein and pocket motion, interaction fingerprints, geometry-event occupancies, and MM-GBSA endpoint binding estimates.
analysis.main_results: BMS-986205 in the W730A mutant showed the lowest mean displacement from its case-specific reference pose (1.86 Å). ERDRP-0519 produced more-negative raw MM-GBSA binding estimates in both wild-type and W730A receptor states. W730A altered static contact annotations and residue-level endpoint terms in a ligand-dependent manner.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate that W730A-dependent remodeling of the inhibitor pocket differentially affects the two chemotypes, with BMS-986205 showing greater structural stability in the mutant. The authors propose BMS-986205 as a structural probe for W730A-dependent pocket remodeling and define testable contact and binding hypotheses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study provides mechanistic insights into Nipah virus polymerase inhibitor resistance and may guide the design of antiviral agents resilient to W730A-mediated pocket remodeling. It also offers experimentally testable hypotheses for optimizing inhibitor binding and specificity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to in silico analyses without experimental validation, which constrains the strength of conclusions about biological relevance. The study’s reliance on computational predictions introduces uncertainty regarding real-world binding dynamics and therapeutic efficacy.

analysis.summary_en: This computational study investigated how the W730 residue in the Nipah virus polymerase inhibitor pocket modulates molecular recognition of two antiviral compounds, BMS-986205 and ERDRP-0519. Using explicit-solvent molecular dynamics and MM-GBSA binding estimates, the authors compared wild-type and W730A mutant polymerase pockets. BMS-986205 exhibited lower displacement in the W730A mutant (1.86 Å), while ERDRP-0519 showed more favorable binding estimates in both receptor states. W730A altered ligand-specific contact patterns and residue-level binding terms, suggesting differential remodeling of the inhibitor pocket. The authors propose BMS-986205 as a structural probe for W730A-dependent changes and outline hypotheses for experimental validation. The findings highlight potential mechanisms of resistance and avenues for designing inhibitors resilient to W730A-mediated remodeling, though the study’s in silico nature limits direct biological inference.
